summary: Defines managed objects related to the forwarding of IP packets in a way that works for both IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces RFC 2096 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard way to ask a router what its address-to-road table looks like.

questions: what is the ip forwarding table mib
how does snmp read a routing table
subtitle: The standard SNMP table for reading, and optionally editing, a router's IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding table.

tldr.problem: The older forwarding table MIB, RFC 2096, only handled IPv4, so network management systems had no common way to inspect routes for both IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4292 defines inetCidrRouteTable, which keeps the structure of the old table but identifies addresses with a type and a value, so one table can hold routes of either IP version.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2096, deprecates the IPv4-only objects, and adds a read-only compliance option for devices that only report routes.

today: RFC 4292 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2096 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4292 defines a part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing objects related to forwarding IP packets, in a way that does not depend on the IP version. MIB objects are generally read and changed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and are written in the Structure of Management Information, here SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).

One limit is stated up front: the MIB does not support several instances for the same address family. It does support one instance per address family.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a shared list of questions a management program may ask a router about where it sends traffic, written in a format every maker agrees on.

sections.title: Three Objects in the Module
sections.content:
The current part of the MIB is small: one table and two global objects.

  • inetCidrRouteNumber is the number of current routes. It exists so a manager does not have to read the whole table just to count it.
  • inetCidrRouteDiscards counts valid routes that were discarded from the table for any reason, for example to free buffer space. It replaces ipRoutingDiscards and ipv6DiscardedRoutes.
  • inetCidrRouteTable shows IP version-independent multipath CIDR routes.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one big list of routes, a counter for how many routes there are, and a counter for how many were thrown away.

sections.title: How It Replaces Older MIBs
sections.content:
The module contains several deprecated and obsolete tables and objects, and the text traces the chain. ipRouteTable came from RFC 1213 and was updated by ipForwardTable in RFC 1354. That was in turn obsoleted by ipCidrRouteTable in RFC 2096, which supports multipath routes with the same network number but different masks.

The ipCidrRouteTable and ipCidrRouteNumber objects are deprecated by this MIB. Likewise ipRoutingDiscards from RFC 2011 and ipv6DiscardedRoutes from RFC 2465 are deprecated in favor of inetCidrRouteDiscards.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new version of the form fixed something in the last one. This newest form works for both kinds of internet addresses, so the old forms are marked as outdated.

sections.title: A Row in the Route Table
sections.content:
Each row describes a particular route to a particular destination under a particular policy. Six index objects identify a row: destination type, destination, prefix length, policy, next-hop type and next hop. The address types come from RFC 4001, which is how one table serves IPv4 and IPv6.

The destination and prefix length must be consistent: the destination ANDed with the mask formed from the prefix length must equal the destination, otherwise a SET or CREATE returns inconsistentName. The policy index is opaque and has no defined meaning; its default value is { 0 0 }. For non-remote routes the next-hop type is unknown(0) and the next hop is a zero-length string.

The other columns are the outgoing interface (inetCidrRouteIfIndex, where 0 means no interface is specified), the route type, the protocol it was learned from, its age in seconds, the next hop's autonomous system number (0 when unknown), five metrics and a row status. A metric that is not used should be set to -1, and what each metric means depends on the routing protocol. A row cannot be modified while its status is active.

If the combined number of elements in destination, policy and next hop exceeds 111, column instance OIDs will have more than 128 sub-identifiers and cannot be accessed using SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is like an index card: where the traffic is going, which exit to use, how far it is, and how the router learned about it.

sections.title: Route Types
sections.content:
The inetCidrRouteType object says what a route does. local means the next hop is the final destination, while remote means it is not. Two types throw traffic away: reject discards it and sends a notification such as an ICMP error to the sender, which some protocols use to aggregate routes correctly, and blackhole discards it silently.

Routes that do not result in forwarding or rejection should not be displayed, even if the implementation stores them internally.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routes point to a neighbour, and some just throw the mail away. One kind tells the sender it was thrown away, and the other says nothing.

sections.title: Full and Read-Only Compliance
sections.content:
Implementations can claim one of two current compliance statements. Full compliance is for implementations that support read-create. It requires support for global and non-global IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and for inetCidrRouteStatus support for createAndWait is not required.

Read-only compliance is for implementations that only wish to retrieve data. It relaxes write access on the writable columns, so a device can report its routes without letting anyone change them. The read-only statement is new in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can say it lets managers both look and change, or only look. Both are allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The route table is critical to the operation of a node, especially a router. Unauthenticated write access can compromise the validity of forwarding information. Reading is also sensitive: the table can be used to map the network in preparation for a denial-of-service attack, and inetCidrRouteProto reveals which routing protocols are in use.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions earlier than SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must also configure access so only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A router's list of routes is like a map of a castle's doors. Only trusted people should be allowed to read it or change it.

items.label: reject
items.desc: Discards traffic and returns an ICMP-style notification.

items.label: local
items.desc: Local interface; the next hop is the final destination.

items.label: remote
items.desc: Remote destination; the next hop is not the final destination.
